newsitem.title: PERU: Peru military swears loyalty amid political crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru military swears loyalty amid political crisis.

text.p: Peru's armed forces pledged their loyalty on Thursday to President Alberto Fujimori as at least two cabinet resignations deepened a political crisis facing the government.

"We want to emphatically express our subordination, loyalty and disciplined support," said armed forces head Gen. Nicolas Bari de Hermoza at a hastily called ceremony in the Government Palace attended by the military top brass.
He added: "Mr. President, you can be absolutely convinced that in the armed forces and national police force, you have the firmest pillars to defend democratic and constitutional institutionality."

A grave-faced Fujimori noted that he and the military had shared "seven long years" and said he was "convinced as always that the armed forces and the national police join together their professionalism and patriotism."
A survey by leading pollster Apoyo S.A. earlier this week showed that 53 percent of Peruvians believe the military is the real power in Peru. Only 38 percent said Fujimori holds the reins.
Fujimori's cabinet suffered another loss on Thursday with the resignation of Defence Minister Gen. Tomas Castillo Meza over alleged rights abuses by the security forces, government sources said.
Castillo's departure, which could not be immediately confirmed by official government spokesmen, followed Wednesday's resignation of Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela.
One of the most respected figures in the cabinet, Tudela was widely believed to have resigned to disassociate himself from a string of embarrassing scandals facing Fujimori.
The sources said the defence post would be filled by Interior Minister Gen. Cesar Saucedo Sanchez, who in turn would be replaced by regional military head Gen. Jose Villanueva Ruesta.
There were unconfirmed versions in local media that Justice Minister Carlos Hermoza Moya had also had a resignation offer accepted by Fujimori.

The cabinet changes added to a political crisis that has seen Fujimori's popularity tumble to its lowest level in seven years of power on growing public outrage over a series of allegations against the government and security forces over corruption and rights abuses.

Particularly damaging were weekend claims of phone-tapping by secret services, and the annulment of Peruvian citizenship for the Israeli-born owner of a local television channel critical of the military.
The allegation believed to have brought Meza's departure was the recent torture of army intelligence agent Leonor La Rosa by colleagues angry at her alleged leaks to the media.

Peru's entire cabinet had made a technical resignation last week as part of a routine annual move ahead of the president's speech to the nation on the July 28 Independence Day. The president normally ratifies his ministers or makes changes on that day.
But analysts said this week's moves showed senior government figures were taking the initiative to resign irrevocably rather than wait for Fujimori's decision.

Just a few blocks away from Thurday's Government Palace ceremony, hundreds of anti-government demonstrators staged a rowdy march chanting "Down With the Dictatorship." The protest was organised by Peru's leading union umbrella organisation, the General Confederation of Workers.
Bari also confirmed Peru was carrying out training exercises on its disputed border with Ecuador, where both countries fought a short war in 1995.
